blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. The dominant interface compresses it into the hidden state of a single [SEG] token, a d-dimensional vector with no spatial index, and leaves the decoder, which never sees the expression, to recover the referent's extent. We show that the VLM already computes a better signal: the [SEG] token's attention over the image tokens, which is defined on the patch grid by construction. Probing a frozen segmentation VLM, we find that this attention yields 18 to 22 more gIoU than the [SEG] hidden state when read by the same probe, that it gains nothing from the image where the hidden state does, and that it is concentrated in the late layers. Building on these findings, we introduce AttnSeg, which replaces the [SEG] embedding with this attention as the decoder's prompt. A learned, signed combination of the attention heads forms a dense spatial prompt, and an attention-guidance objective supervises it directly. A two-stage recipe first trains the VLM to localize without the decoder, then trains the decoder to refine, within the budget of standard fine-tuning. Applied to Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg by 6.4 gIoU and GS-Eval by 10.2 at 4B (4.2 and 9.6 over the same model fine-tuned on the same data), and by 8.8 and 11.3 at 14B. The gains reach 13 to 18 gIoU on object parts, multiple objects, and single objects, where the referent must be singled out, and are negligible on stuff regions, which the decoder already recovers unaided. Code and models are available at https://eslambakr.github.io/attseg_project_page/

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Segmenting an object from a natural-language expression requires deciding which region the expression refers to and where exactly its boundary
lies. Promptable segmenters such as SAM ( Kirillov et al., 2023 ) , HQ-SAM ( Ke et al., 2023 ) and SAM3 ( Carion et al., 2026 ) have made the second the easier
half of the problem: given a prompt that points at the right region, they return a
high-quality mask. The first requires understanding the expression, which is the
role of a vision-language model (VLM). This division of labor motivates the hypothesis at the center of our work: the VLM should be the load-bearing
localizer, and the decoder should only refine. Whether this holds depends on the interface , the representation through
which the VLM passes the referent’s location to the decoder.

blocks.en:
The [SEG] interface, however, reduces the entire spatial message to a single d d -dimensional vector with no spatial index, and the decoder that receives it
never sees the expression. A vector can point at the referent, but it cannot
specify its granularity: for the left ear of the dog , a pointer to the dog
leaves the decoder to guess whether the dog, its head or its ear is meant. The
vector is also supervised only through the mask loss computed after the decoder,
so nothing requires the VLM to carry the localization, and the decoder absorbs as
much of it as it can. The released Sa2VA-4B illustrates the consequence. On
GS-Eval ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , it reaches 90.8 90.8 gIoU on stuff regions,
which the decoder can recover from almost any prompt, but only 49.8 49.8 on single
objects and 17.8 17.8 on object parts. This raises a question: does the VLM
already compute a better representation of where the referent lies, and can the
decoder be prompted with it directly?

blocks.en:
Building on these findings, we introduce AttnSeg , which replaces the [SEG] embedding
with the [SEG] token’s attention as the decoder’s prompt
(Figure 1 c). A learned 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution with signed weights
combines the per-head maps into a single map, emphasizing the informative late
heads and subtracting those that attend to sinks or distractors, and the map enters
the decoder’s dense prompt channel without being thresholded or sampled. An
attention-guidance objective supervises this map directly. We adopt a weighted
cosine, which asks for the referent’s full extent and penalizes concentrated
misplaced attention most. Training proceeds in two stages within the budget of a
single epoch: the VLM first learns to localize under the attention-guidance
objective, without the decoder, and the decoder is then trained to refine the
frozen map. Prior systems derive sparse point prompts from attention or similarity
maps ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) ; AttnSeg instead reads the [SEG] token’s own attention, keeps it dense, and trains the VLM to shape it.

blocks.en:
In summary, our contributions are threefold: • A probing analysis that compares, within a frozen segmentation VLM, the two
spatial signals of the [SEG] token. It shows that the attention carries
considerably more localization than the hidden state the dominant interface
transmits, and that this localization is concentrated in the late layers. • AttnSeg , which replaces the [SEG] embedding with a learned, signed combination
of the [SEG] token’s attention maps as a dense decoder prompt, supervised by an
attention-guidance objective and trained in two stages that make the VLM the
localizer and the decoder a refiner, within the budget of standard finetuning. • Consistent improvements at two scales on ReasonSeg and GS-Eval, concentrated
on the splits where the referent must be singled out, with analyses
showing that the attention-guidance objective accounts for most of the gain and makes the attention directly readable.

blocks.en: 3 Methodology
blocks.zh: 3 方法

blocks.en:
This section derives AttnSeg from an analysis of the model it builds on.
Section 3.1 formalizes language-guided segmentation with a VLM
and a promptable decoder, and states our hypothesis about the interface between
the two. Section 3.2 tests that hypothesis by probing a frozen
segmentation VLM, which reveals two properties of its [SEG] token: its attention
over the image encodes considerably more localization than its hidden state, and
this localization is concentrated in the late layers, while the early layers carry
almost none.
Building on these findings, Section 3.3 introduces AttnSeg ,
which replaces the [SEG] embedding with the attention, combines the attention
heads through a learned aggregation, and supervises the result with an
attention-guidance objective in a decoupled, two-stage training.

blocks.en: 3.1 Problem Setup and Hypothesis
blocks.zh: 3.1 问题设置和假设

blocks.en:
The predominant approach to language-guided segmentation pairs a vision-language
model (VLM), which interprets the referring expression, with a promptable
segmentation decoder such as SAM ( Kirillov et al., 2023 ; Ravi et al., 2025 ) , which
produces the segmentation mask (Figure 1 b).

Under Eq. ( 1 ), the VLM’s role is to indicate where the
referent lies. A pointer suffices when the referent coincides with a region the
decoder can delineate on its own, such as a large, contiguous stuff region, but
it falls short when the expression specifies which object, or which part of it,
is meant.
For instance, given “ the left ear of the dog ”, a representation that
points at the dog does not determine whether the intended region is the dog, its head or its ear.
Promptable decoders are ambiguous in precisely this way, which is why SAM predicts
several nested masks for a single point prompt ( Kirillov et al., 2023 ) . Since 𝒟 \mathcal{D} has no access to 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , it cannot resolve the ambiguity from
the expression and must fall back on the granularity its training data made most
likely. We therefore hypothesize that compressing the referent into 𝒉 seg \bm{h}_{\textsc{seg}} discards spatial information the VLM has already computed.

blocks.en:
To validate our hypothesis, we employ probing, the established practice of
training a lightweight classifier on a network’s frozen internal representations
to measure what information they encode ( Alain & Bengio, 2018 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) . We freeze Sa2VA-4B ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) entirely, discard its decoder, and train only a probe that
predicts the ground-truth mask from a single internal signal. Since the model is
frozen, any accuracy the probe attains reflects information the signal already
carries. Two signals are compared: the stacked attention maps 𝒂 \bm{a} of
Eq. ( 2 ), and the [SEG] hidden state at every layer, mapped onto the
patch grid by a learned projection shared by all embedding probes. Because a
sufficiently expressive probe can learn the task itself rather than read it from
the representation ( Hewitt & Liang, 2019 ) , each signal is read at two
capacities (Table 5 ): a single 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution
( ≈ 5 {\approx}5 K parameters) and a U-Net ( ≈ 3.86 {\approx}3.86 M). The shared projection
alone costs ≈ 672 {\approx}672 K parameters, far more than the convolutional attention
probe, so any capacity mismatch favors the embedding. Appendix B gives the architectures and training details, and Section 4.3 repeats the procedure on the trained model.

Figure 2(a) compares the two signals at both capacities. With
the U-Net, the attention reaches 53.2 53.2 gIoU on GS-Eval ( Hu et al., 2025 ) and 52.1 52.1 on ReasonSeg ( Lai et al., 2024 ) , against 35.0 35.0 and 30.6 30.6 for the [SEG] hidden state. With the single convolution, by contrast, the two signals score
within a few points of each other, so the attention’s advantage appears only once
the probe can combine its channels nonlinearly. This is consistent with prior
observations that localization is carried by a small number of heads, while much
of the remaining attention mass collects on uninformative sink tokens ( Kang et al., 2025b ; Kang et al., 2025a ) : the signal is present,
but it must be selected and combined before it can be read.

Having established that the attention is the stronger signal, we ask where in the

a property of the model rather than of the probe. A uniform average would
therefore spend most of its weight on layers that carry no localization; together
with the concentration of localization in a few heads, this motivates the learned
aggregation of Section 3.3 .

Motivated by these findings, AttnSeg replaces the [SEG] embedding with the [SEG] token’s attention as the interface between the VLM and the decoder. Instead of
compressing the referent into 𝒉 seg \bm{h}_{\textsc{seg}} , it combines the per-head maps of
Eq. ( 2 ) into one map 𝒂 ^ \hat{\bm{a}} and prompts the decoder with it alone: 𝒀 ^ = 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝑰 , 𝒂 ^ ) , 𝒂 ^ = ∑ l = 1 L ∑ k = 1 H w l , k ​ 𝒂 ( l , k ) ∈ ℝ h × w , w l , k ( 0 ) = 1 L ​ H . \hat{\bm{Y}}=\mathcal{D}\big(\bm{I},\hat{\bm{a}}\big),\qquad\hat{\bm{a}}=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{k=1}^{H}w_{l,k}\,\bm{a}^{(l,k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w},\qquad w_{l,k}^{(0)}=\tfrac{1}{LH}. (3) Compared with Eq. ( 1 ), the decoder now receives a map defined on the image grid rather than a d d -dimensional vector.
The map enters through the decoder’s dense mask-prompt channel and it is never thresholded or sampled, so the decoder receives its graded confidence rather than a binarized mask or a handful of points (Appendix C ).
The weights w w amount to a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution over the L ​ H LH maps and add only L ​ H LH parameters. Their form follows from Section 3.2 : localization is concentrated in a few late heads, so the combination must be selective, and it is learned rather than fixed to the band we measured, which would otherwise have to be located anew for every backbone. Initialized at the uniform average, the combination starts from the plain head mean and departs from it only where training finds a better weighting.
The weights are also unconstrained in sign: a softmax gate, whose weights lie on the simplex, can only suppress a misleading head, whereas a negative weight can subtract it.
Appendix C gives a second reason to prefer the convolution.

blocks.en:

baseline of Section 4.3 .

split of ReasonSeg ( Lai et al., 2024 ) names the target by its function or its role in the scene

accumulates intersection and union over the whole set, is dominated by a small

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We revisited the interface through which a vision-language model passes the
location of its referent to a segmentation decoder. Probing a frozen segmentation
VLM showed that the [SEG] token’s attention carries considerably more localization
than the hidden state the dominant interface transmits, and that this localization
is concentrated in the late layers. AttnSeg builds on these findings: it prompts the
decoder with a learned, signed combination of the [SEG] token’s attention maps in
place of its embedding, supervises that map with an attention-guidance objective,
and trains in two stages that make the VLM the localizer and the decoder a
refiner, within the budget of standard finetuning. At both scales and on both
benchmarks, the gains concentrate on object parts, multiple objects and single
objects, where the referent must be singled out, and are negligible on stuff
regions the decoder recovers unaided. More broadly, our results suggest that
a segmentation VLM already computes where its referent lies, and that the decisive
design choice is to pass that computation to the decoder in the form in which it is
made, and to supervise it there.

blocks.en: Ethics statement
blocks.zh: 道德操守说明

blocks.en:
This work studies the interface between a vision-language model and a promptable
mask decoder. It involves no human subjects and no new data collection: every
dataset and benchmark we use is public and is used as released, under its own
license and evaluation protocol, and both models we build on are publicly
released checkpoints.

许可和评估协议, 而我们开发的两种模式都是公开的

blocks.en:
Two risks are worth stating plainly. First, our method deliberately moves the
localization burden onto the language model, which means the system’s errors
become the language model’s errors. It inherits whatever biases the base model
carries in deciding which object a description refers to, and a sharper, more
confident attention map can make a confidently wrong choice of referent harder
for the decoder to correct rather than easier. An improvement in gIoU on the
benchmarks we report is not evidence that the model resolves ambiguous or
contested descriptions correctly, and we would not deploy it in a safety-critical
setting without task-specific validation. Second, a system that segments
arbitrary objects from free-form language lowers the barrier to fine-grained
visual search, and carries the dual-use considerations that come with it.

SAM ( Kirillov et al., 2023 ) produces a mask at 1024 1024 px from a prompt, and SAM2 ( Ravi et al., 2025 ) extends it to video with a memory bank that propagates a mask
from a few conditioning frames. Its prompt encoder handles points and boxes sparsely , as positional embeddings concatenated to the decoder’s query

PolyFormer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) cast referring segmentation as sequential
polygon generation before large language models entered the field, regressing

prediction through a single language interface. VisionLLM’s own successor ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , however, reintroduces task-specific decoders.

Four structural reasons account for the gap. The output resolution is the
language model’s coarse patch grid. A token cross-entropy penalizes a vertex that

shift rewrites many tokens, so small spatial errors become large token errors.
Finally, a single mispredicted early vertex distorts the remainder of the contour.

route: it emits the box and points of a SAM prompt as text, so the decoder is
prompted without a dedicated segmentation token.

Kang et al. (2025b) explain why attention-based localization has
looked unreliable: averaging heads gives sparse, noisy maps, whereas a few localization heads track the referent consistently. They isolate these
heads with two criteria, an attention sum that keeps heads placing enough of their
attention on the image and a spatial entropy over the connected components of the binarized map
that keeps heads whose mass forms one compact cluster, and rank heads by how often
they are among the ten lowest-entropy heads over 1,000 1{,}000 image-text pairs. That
selection is made offline and then frozen, whereas the aggregation of

the model answers wrongly, which supports passing the map to the decoder directly and
cautions against treating map sharpness as a proxy for task accuracy.
